vector and full-text search built on object storage: fast, 10x cheaper, and extremely scalable

A former Shopify search colleague vouches for founder Simon ("he knows his sh*t"). He says his ideal is a cloud service that supplies retrieval and lets him express ranking fluently, like Polars dataframe math (lexical/embedding similarity, recency/popularity boosts, reranking features), then stays out of his way.
Commenter loves the object-storage-first approach, calling it a natural fit for the cloud.
Comparison: one commenter says turbopuffer sounds like a source-unavailable version of Quickwit, a criticism that it is not open source.

Pushback on turbopuffer's claim that 2022-era production vector DBs relied on in-memory storage: pg_vector predates that, doesn't require in-memory storage, and can handle vector search over 100m+ documents with decent performance.

Two commenters say the article's ClickHouse figures are wrong. They describe them as "woefully disappointing and incorrect" and say ClickHouse read latency is ≤100ms and write latency ≤1s, not ≥1s/minutes. One adds that ClickHouse also suits logging, real-time analytics and RAG.

Critique of the cost argument against RAM ($3600/TB/month): at Hetzner the commenter pays $200/TB/month for RAM, 18x cheaper. They suggest you can reach the goal with less complexity by dropping the marked-up part.
The long introductory page "has a ton of very juicy data in it, even if you don't care about the product itself." Another commenter praised the website's aesthetic.

Commenter who has seen very large Elasticsearch deployments says throwing everything into S3 would be "incredible" and useful beyond vector search. They ask whether the approach could be built on open-source Lucene or whether the indexes are proprietary.
A commenter questions the use case, asking whether these operations are really too intensive for normal servers/VMs. They also call "Turbopuffer" a terrible name for its sexual/weed connotations.
